reviews.review:
I have to say, I didn't go into my cold war turn-based tactics game expecting to be a high school girl in some jock guy's harem. I'm not complaining, but I am surprised.

This is a game that, I feel, has a fairly good idea and a fairly 'meh' execution. I wouldn't say I *don't* recommend, but literally every review for this right now is positive, so I'd like to give the consumer my gripes with it so they can make a more balanced purchasing decision.

Missile Command Delta is a combination of the tactical gameplay you'll see in the trailer (with light deckbuilding elements) and an exploration game with light visual novel elements. My opinion of the tactical gameplay is reasonably good, 7-ish out of ten, probably scratches a specific niche few mainstream titles do.

I'm generally ambivalent or disappointed with everything that *isn't* that tactical gameplay.

This sounds fairly harsh. But a lot of the game's quality, I feel, is kind of front-loaded. And a lot of the misgivings I had didn't really become apparent to me until about halfway through my playthrough. The more I played this game, the more comparisons I drew to Dangagnronpa, which is a game I think is arguably best-in-slot for a lot of the areas that this one flounders in.

My first gripe regarding this turn-based tactics, choose-your-own-adventure, exploration game is the exploration. A lot of this game's environments are very samey. Very similary floorplans, very similar color pallet, lots of confined spaces and hallways. This sounds like a knitpick, but a core premise of the game is starting in a relatively confined space, unlocking new areas, and progressing deeper in this underground missile bunker you've found. 

This is kind of a bigger problem than you might think, because you'll be running around that small area a lot looking for clues and solving puzzles. You sprint fairly slowly, and you retrace the same ground a lot, and it all kinda blends together for me. Clover Pit, buckshot roulette,  and Inscription are three games that take place almost entirely in a single room. But they're visually interesting and are built around maximizing the effect of that confined space. Danganronpa, like this game, starts in a fairly confined part of a building and slowly opens up. But each new area is visually distinct, which lends itself to a sense of progression solely through the environment.

Missile Command doesn't feel like it tries to do either of this to me. The level design feels like it's solely there to break up the puzzles and the tactical gameplay. This would be fine if the game didn't make me spend so much time in it. We do finally start seeing some more interesting spaces in the climax of the game, but the other 95% of the time you're running through three floors that are remarkably similar or crawling through air vents. The game tries to amend this somewhat by having you move through those rooms with no power, or after they've been damaged, but it doesn't feel enough to make discovering new areas feel exciting to me. The third level has some elements of the environment tied to its puzzles, but it also makes you run around so much in that otherwise-samey area that the main character lampshades it.

Level *transitions*, admittedly, are done reasonably well. There's multiple ways to traverse levels, and the game's plot makes you use different ones. 

I think puzzles are overused. There's a couple unique ones, but there's also two that I felt like repeated enough that it became annoying.

The pacing for this game feels really weird to me. The beginning third feels like it had the most variety of puzzles, exploration, and things to do. Then it starts feeling like it's getting more dynamic and might be building up to something before absolutely dragging along. Then the climax comes and it's fun and somewhat intense again out of seemingly nowhere. Like, I didn't know I was about to enter the climax until the game explicitly told me this was the point of no return, because it didn't feel like I was building towards anything emotionally for me.

Characters feel really weak. I'm honestly kind of surprised they included them at all. The storytelling is done through a combination of character dialogue, flashbacks/dream sequences, and random notes you find lying around (similar to the voicemail system in FEAR). I got an achievement for maxing the relationship with my goth-trans-girl best friend and the only thing I really knew about her by the end was that she was trans, had issues with her dad, and liked music. It's fine for characters to just be there as quest-givers, but the game tries to pretend like they aren't with these dialogue branches where you get to pick sides when they fight. There's a lot of these Evangelion-esque dream montages where the game tries to leverage some emotional weight, but it all feels really goofy and unearned to me. I was learning about who my friends were through a flashback montage at the end of the game, which feels like an unusual choice. 

The notes and such feel weird too. Like, not that they're purposely self-aware, but like the writers know there's supposed to be a story in the game so they're making game prose rather than creating breadcrumbs for an organic narrative. 

Music during setpiece moments is pretty good. Music during spooky moments is pretty good. Music during everything else is just okay. You spend a sizeable chunk of the game during 'everything else'.

Outside a few brief segments, I never felt like there were any stakes in this game, or any real motivation to explore deeper, until the climax. Like, one moment you're sneaking around this guy's back because you think he's dangerous and the next moment you're opening an air vent and crawling into it right in front of him. One moment a suspected murder is freaking out at you calling you a traitor and the next you end the dialogue tree and just walk away. You're going to be playing training simulations around 4x as often as real missions, because that's what unlocks all your doors for some reason, so most of the combat has no real stakes. 

There's a mystery. I didn't find it very well-developed. I feel like I was kind of just told there was a mystery and was expected to speculate about it without any real interplay with the gameplay. The saucy elements I did like were resolved about halfway into my playthrough and was something of a letdown. There was a strong opportunity for a System Shock-style character deception or plot interplay with the fact that you're informed early on in the game that you're under surveillance, but the execution feels 'meh' to me. 

I got the true ending. The climax segment and the ending path I chose was fairly enjoyable, and the music and plot twist felt like it was an okay emotional resolution. It also felt kind of silly though once I stopped to think about it.

I only encountered one bug during my playthrough. It didn't effect gameplay. This is praiseworthy.

All told, I think i'd rate the tactical portion of the game 6-7/10, the puzzle elements 5/10, the exploration 4/10, and the plot 3-4/10. For a combined overall weighted score of about 5/10. I absolutely think credit should be awarded for trying to mix genres like this into something cohesive. I don't feel scammed or ripped off. But having finished my playthrough, I don't think I'll have a strong desire to play it again or get different endings, and I would have enjoyed playing something else more. 

5/10, an okay game. I think the tactics game stands on its own. I don't think the puzzles, plot, or exploration stand on their own, and that's half the game. 

I see a lot of people claiming to enjoy the elements of the game I was less favorable towards. I do not think those opinions are *wrong*, and I can absolutely see some of these elements being weighted differently by other people. But I do think there is value in a potential buyer being able to weigh a dissenting opinion before purchasing, so here's mine.
